segments.spokenText: Part 2. An orientation talk at a community arts centre. You now have one minute to read questions 11 to 20.

Welcome to everyone starting a course at the Foundry Arts Centre. The building was once a small factory, but its new name isn't an invitation to operate industrial equipment. We run practical arts courses for adults, and some family sessions during school holidays. Today I'll describe five activities you may want to try and then explain how the centre works. You don't have to decide everything this morning. The aim is to help you understand which course fits the time and experience you actually have.

segments.spokenText: First, bookbinding. This starts next week and lasts four Tuesday evenings. Materials are provided, but we require a reservation because the tutor prepares a separate pack for each person. Turning up on the first evening and hoping to find an empty chair won't work, even if someone is absent. We can often offer a place on the next course instead.

segments.spokenText: The lunchtime sketch group is quite different. There is no advance booking and no expectation that you already draw well. Its special arrangement is that it's held outside the centre, in the covered market across the road. The group meets under the market clock. This gives people moving subjects to draw, and traders have agreed that participants may sit along the wall without blocking customers.

segments.spokenText: For textile printing, you should bring something of your own to print on. A plain cotton bag is ideal; a smooth T-shirt is another possibility. We provide inks and tools, but not the fabric item itself. Please avoid a favourite expensive garment for your first experiment. The tutor will explain why different surfaces absorb colour differently.

segments.spokenText: Our percussion session has been moved to an earlier time. People used to arrive at seven on Wednesdays; it now begins at six, because the neighbouring room is needed for a quiet class later in the evening. That's a permanent change for this term, not just for the first week.

segments.spokenText: Finally, the clay modelling course allows children to attend, provided an adult takes the course with them. It isn't a supervised drop-off club. Both people make something and can help each other. If you were hoping to work completely on your own, choose the adults-only session on the other day.

segments.spokenText: Now for some general information. Membership fees cover the shared studio space and basic maintenance. They don't cover every course material. We used to charge one inclusive fee, but someone taking only sketching was helping pay for expensive clay. Separating the costs makes the arrangement more transparent, even though the price list is slightly longer.

segments.spokenText: Our noticeboard displays examples of work, but you don't have to agree to public display. Some people enjoy sharing a first attempt; others want to practise privately. Ask the tutor to mark your work as not for display. That decision will have no effect on your access to future courses or the amount of help you receive.

segments.spokenText: Equipment may stay in the studio between sessions, but unfinished pieces must have a name and date. Unlabelled work is difficult to store responsibly because staff can't tell whether it has been abandoned. We won't throw things away immediately. After a published storage period, we'll contact the maker where possible and clear space for current classes.

segments.spokenText: The café next door offers a small discount to course members on weekday afternoons. It is independent of the centre, so please raise food orders with café staff rather than a tutor. We mention it because many students like to continue talking after class, not because a café purchase is part of membership.

segments.spokenText: Please tell us if you need adjustments to take part. The best time is when you book, because some arrangements require planning. However, if you discover a difficulty during a session, speak to the tutor then. We don't expect you to predict every problem in advance. The office can discuss an alternative rather than simply telling you to wait until the next term.
